findings.summary: The caption's first sentence is a series label rather than a hook, burying the actual hook in sentence two.
findings.evidence: "Part 2 of BASH TRAPS & SIGNALS. Your script creates a temp dir, then dies to Ctrl-C — and leaves the mess behind."
findings.fix: Lead with the hook and demote the label: "Your script creates a temp dir, then dies to Ctrl-C — and leaves the mess behind. Part 2 of BASH TRAPS & SIGNALS. This handbook is the full field guide..."

findings.summary: The claim that a subshell copies traps is wrong — caught traps are reset to default in a subshell, which the part's own page-2 table states correctly.
findings.evidence: Page 1: "A subshell is a forked copy of the whole shell" / "Variables, traps and options are copied, not shared" — contradicted on page 2 by the Fork Reset Rule table: "caught (`trap f INT`) → default". Bash manual: a subshell environment "is a duplicate of the shell environment, except that traps caught by the shell are reset to the values the shell inherited from its parent at invocation."
findings.fix: Change the bullet to "Variables and options are copied; caught traps are reset to default (ignored signals stay ignored)" so page 1 agrees with the page-2 table.

findings.summary: The set -e/ERR exemption for `&&` and `||` is stated too broadly: the command following the final `&&`/`||` is NOT exempt.
findings.evidence: Page 1: "NOT in `if`/`while` conditions, `&&`/`||` operands, `!`-negated"; repeated page 2: "Skipped inside `if`, `while`, `&&`, `||`, and after `!`". Bash manual: the shell does not exit if the failure is "part of any command executed in a && or || list except the command following the final && or ||". So `true && false` does exit and does fire ERR, while `false && true` does not.
findings.fix: Qualify both bullets: "…`&&`/`||` operands *except the command after the final operator* — `true && false` still fires."

findings.summary: The opening code block uses `set -Eeuo pipefail` before `-E` (and `-u`) are defined; `-E` is only explained on pages 2–3.
findings.evidence: Page 1 code: `set -Eeuo pipefail` / `trap 'echo "FAIL line $LINENO: $BASH_COMMAND (rc=$?)" >&2' ERR`. The meaning of `-E` first appears on page 2 (`"`-E`","ERR inherits","never"` and the "Functions Lose ERR" callout) and page 3 ("`set -E` (errtrace): ERR reaches functions, `$()`, subshells").
findings.fix: Add a bullet on page 1, before or immediately after the code block, stating that ERR traps are not inherited by functions, `$(...)`, or subshells without `set -E` (errtrace) — which is why the example uses `-E` — and note `-u` = unset is fatal.

findings.summary: dash does not silently ignore an ERR trap — it reports `trap: ERR: bad trap` and, trap being a special builtin, aborts the script.
findings.evidence: "`dash` and `sh` ignore it silently — no warning". dash's trap builtin rejects unknown signal names: `dash: 1: trap: ERR: bad trap` (see ShellCheck SC3047 "In POSIX sh, trapping ERR is undefined" and the widely reported dash error message).
findings.fix: Rewrite as: "`dash` rejects it outright — `trap: ERR: bad trap`, and as a special-builtin error it kills the script; other shells may accept-and-never-fire. Either way the diagnostics you wrote never run."

findings.summary: The recommended `mktemp -d -t app.XX` template is rejected by GNU mktemp, which requires at least three consecutive X's.
findings.evidence: Table row: ["`mktemp -d -t app.XX`","`/tmp/$$` names"]. GNU coreutils mktemp: "TEMPLATE must contain at least 3 consecutive 'X's in last component"; otherwise it exits with `mktemp: too few X's in template 'app.XX'`.
findings.fix: Use `mktemp -d -t app.XXXXXX` (matching the working page-4 skeleton `mktemp -d -t iolar.XXXXXX`).

findings.summary: Page 1 ends with a headingless bullets block defining what a subshell is, orphaned under a sidebox about `|| true`.
findings.evidence: Final page 1 block, immediately after the "Opting Out On Purpose" sidebox: "A subshell is a forked copy of the whole shell / Variables, traps and options are copied, not shared / Nothing set inside can reach back to the parent".
findings.fix: Move these three bullets to the top of page 2 under a heading such as "What A Subshell Is", so the definition opens the fork material instead of trailing the ERR page unlabelled.

findings.summary: The PIPESTATUS clobbering claim is asserted with no example; the demonstrating code sits a page later among unrelated strict-mode blocks.
findings.evidence: Page 1: "`PIPESTATUS` holds every element's status" / "Read it immediately — the next command clobbers it". The only example, `rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}  # curl's` with note "read it before the next command", is on page 2.
findings.fix: Move the `set -o pipefail` / `curl … | jq .id` / `rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}` code block to page 1 directly under the "Pipelines Hide Failures" bullets.

findings.summary: `$BASH_COMMAND` is used in two handler examples but never defined anywhere in the part.
findings.evidence: Page 1 code: `trap 'echo "FAIL line $LINENO: $BASH_COMMAND (rc=$?)" >&2' ERR`; page 4 sidebox: "`trap 'echo D: $BASH_COMMAND' DEBUG` traces before the failure".
findings.fix: Add a clause on page 1 defining `$BASH_COMMAND` as the command currently executing (the one that just failed, inside an ERR trap), alongside the existing `$?`/`$LINENO`/`${BASH_SOURCE[0]}` bullet.

findings.summary: "Never fires your ERR trap" overstates the no-errtrace case: the trap still fires in the calling shell on the non-zero status of the function call or command substitution.
findings.evidence: Tip callout: "Without `set -E`, a failure inside a function, `$(...)` or subshell never fires your ERR trap". Bash manual: the ERR trap is not *inherited* by functions/subshells without errtrace, but the failing `f` or `x=$(false)` is itself a command returning non-zero in the trapped shell, so the handler runs there.
findings.fix: Say what is actually lost: "Without `set -E` the trap isn't inherited, so the handler runs (if at all) at the call site — `$LINENO`/`$BASH_COMMAND` point at the function call, not the line that failed inside it."

findings.evidence: Code line "rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}  # curl's" has the pink pin head overlapping the comment text "curl's" at roughly x=865, y=1185, and the yellow note "read it before the next command" sits over the code block's lower-right area.
findings.fix: Move the pin/sticky-note anchor down and right so it clears the last code line (or shorten the code block's right padding), the way the equivalent notes sit clear of the code on slides 1, 5, and 6.

findings.summary: The skeleton's cleanup never re-raises the caught signal, so the 130/143 exit statuses the part tells you to assert cannot occur with this handler.
findings.evidence: Page 5 cleanup ends `exit "$rc"` where `rc=$?` on entry, but page 6 requires "Re-raise every caught signal: `trap - \"$sig\"; kill -\"$sig\" \"$$\"` … Gives 130 for INT, 143 for TERM" and page 7 says "`kill -TERM` it from another terminal … Assert … status is 143". With a bare `exit "$rc"`, a TERM delivered only to the script exits with the last command's status (often 0), not 143.
findings.fix: Add the re-raise to the shown cleanup, e.g. after `trap - EXIT INT TERM HUP` and the `rm`, `if [ -n "${sig:-}" ]; then kill -"$sig" "$$"; else exit "$rc"; fi`, or trap signals via a wrapper that calls `kill -"$sig" "$$"` after cleanup.

findings.summary: The cleanup disarms only `EXIT INT TERM` while the skeleton traps HUP as well, leaving the re-entry hole the part warns about.
findings.evidence: Page 4 skeleton: "trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM HUP"; page 5 cleanup: "trap - EXIT INT TERM"; page 5 sidebox: "No disarm → a signal re-enters cleanup mid-run". A HUP arriving during cleanup still re-enters it.
findings.fix: Make the disarm list match the arm list: `trap - EXIT INT TERM HUP` (and the same on page 6's handler contract).
